_comment: LEAFNET approved four-class, single-label visual classification taxonomy. DO NOT change these classes without formal research-methodology approval. Sources are cited per class; see docs/dataset.md and Phase2_Status.md.

task.note: Visual classification only - NOT biological diagnosis.

classes.name: healthy
classes.label: Healthy
classes.description: Leaf shows no visible symptoms of rust, leaf spot, blight, pest feeding, or other abnormality.
visual_indicators: Uniform green coloration appropriate to leaf age
No necrotic spots, pustules, chlorotic halos, or lesions
Intact leaf margins and surface texture
Natural senescence yellowing on very old leaves may still qualify if uniform and free of disease symptoms
classes.annotation_guidance: Label healthy only when NO symptom of any disease class is visible. When in doubt between healthy and an early-stage condition, use the uncertain/needs-review path.
confounding_conditions: Early-stage infections may show no symptoms yet (leaf appears healthy)
evidence_sources: Frontiers in Plant Science (2023): mulberry leaf-disease dataset annotated by sericulture experts distinguishes disease-free leaves from rust and spot
Bangladesh Sericulture Development Board expert-annotated criteria (as documented in Frontiers 2023, doi:10.3389/fpls.2023.1175515)

classes.name: leaf_rust
classes.label: Leaf Rust
classes.description: Rust disease of mulberry caused by rust fungi (principally Cerotelium fici; also Peridiopsora/Aecidium mori), visually characterized by raised powdery pustules.
visual_indicators: Early: small yellowish chlorotic spots on the UPPER leaf surface, before pustules erupt on the other side
Erumpent (cuticle-piercing) orange/reddish-brown/yellow-orange POWDERY pustules of spores; tiny (sub-millimetre to ~1 mm), often with a yellowish halo, darkening as they mature
Pustules concentrated on the ABAXIAL (lower) surface, opposite the upper chlorotic spots; light-brown pustule form also documented
Advanced stages: pustules coalesce into a fine yellow-orange spore 'powder' over the leaf; leaves yellow and prematurely wither/fall
classes.annotation_guidance: The key discriminator vs leaf_spot is the POWDERY/RAISED PUSTULE appearance (erupted spore mass). Flat necrotic spots are leaf_spot, not rust. Lower-surface check matters: if only upper chlorotic spots are visible, look for powdery pustules on the underside before labelling. If only early upper spots are present without pustules, flag as uncertain.
confounding_conditions: Early leaf_spot lesions look like the initial pinhead spots of rust
Necrotic spots after pustules rupture can resemble leaf_spot
Insect galls or scale insects can mimic pustules
Coalesced rust pustules form necrotic patches that resemble spot/blight at a glance
evidence_sources: Mordue (1991), CAB Descriptions of Fungi and Bacteria: Aecidium mori, 'Rust of mulberry'

California Pest Rating Proposal for Cerotelium fici (2026): on Ficus carica begins as small yellowish upper-surface spots; reddish-brown to orange uredinial pustules develop primarily on the lower surface opposite the spots; lesions become angular/brown/necrotic; heavy infection -> yellowing and premature defoliation; also documented on M. nigra (Goncalves 2023) and M. alba (Baiyewu 2005)
Solano-Baez et al. (2017): angular necrotic upper-surface lesions with reddish-brown erumpent lower-surface pustules; premature defoliation

Goncalves et al. (2023), Plant Disease 107:2259 (doi:10.1094/PDIS-11-22-2656-PDN): first report of C. fici on Morus nigra in Brazil - light brown pustules with yellowish halos, leaf yellowing, premature leaf fall at high severity

Baiyewu et al. (2005), Pakistan J. Plant Pathology: occurrence of leaf rust of mulberry (Morus alba, Nigeria) by Cerotelium fici - pinhead brownish-black eruptive spots, then yellowing and premature withering
Dev Maji (2011): epidemiology of brown leaf rust caused by Peridiopsora mori
Kasuya et al. (2024), Mycoscience: Gymnosporangium mori comb. nov. taxonomy

classes.name: leaf_spot
classes.label: Leaf Spot
classes.description: Necrotic spotting diseases of mulberry leaves caused by diverse fungi (Cercospora moricola, Pseudocercospora mori, Mycosphaerella/Phloeospora maculans, Bipolaris, Curvularia, and others), visually characterized by flat, discrete necrotic spots.
visual_indicators: Discrete, FLAT necrotic spots: small dark brown/black dots to larger (~0.5-3+ cm) dry circular or irregular lesions
Spots often have pale/grey centers with dark borders and/or diffuse chlorotic (yellow) halos
'Target/eyespot' morphology (Cercospora/Mycosphaerella morphotype): centres fade WHITISH/GREY while a distinct dark-brown-to-black necrotic margin remains
Tiny dark brown-black acervuli (spore fruiting bodies) may dot the lesion centres (Mycosphaerella/Phloeospora)
Grey leaf spot (Pseudocercospora mori): jet-black to dark-grey round/ovoid lesions ~2-10 mm, frequently merging into larger patches; greyish mold-like or sooty patches possible
Vein-limited angular spots occur in some pathogens (Phloeospora)
Severe cases: spots coalesce, leaves yellow and drop prematurely
classes.annotation_guidance: Label leaf_spot when flat necrotic lesions dominate and no raised powdery pustules (rust) or large spreading dead areas (blight) are present. Species-level identification is NOT possible visually; the class deliberately groups multiple fungal pathogens. Note documented sources disagree on whether merged spot lesions belong with spot or blight - use the halo/water-soaked-margin tests below and the needs_review path where ambiguous.
confounding_conditions: Rust before pustule formation produces similar pinhead necrotic spots
Coalesced leaf-spot lesions produce a 'blighted' appearance (documented for Bipolaris sorokiniana and Pseudocercospora grey leaf spot)
Physical damage and insect feeding can leave necrotic-looking marks
Herbicide/nutrient burn can cause necrotic flecking
Bacterial leaf spot / blight (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) produces small angular black spots that overlap the spot class profile (see leaf_blight)
evidence_sources: Arunakumar et al. (2023), BMC/PMC10665727: diversity of fungal pathogens in leaf spot of Indian mulberry; symptomatology per pathogen

Frontiers in Plant Science (2025): Pseudocercospora mori grey leaf spot of mulberry, Guangdong China - jet-black to dark-grey round/irregular/oval lesions 2-10 mm that merge into larger patches; greyish mold-like patches, black sooty spots, light grey areas, powdery dark grey coatings

RHS: 'Mulberry leaf spot (Mycosphaerella mori, syn. Phloeospora mori)' - small dark brown irregular spots with pale-green/yellow haloes; centres become whitish with brown necrotic margins; tiny brown-black acervuli on lesions; lesions merge to affect larger areas under severe attacks
Hawaii CTAHR PD-41 (Cercospora leaf spot of coffee as morphotype reference): circular spots with tan/gray/white centres - the classic Cercospora 'target/eyespot' lesion
Soylu et al. (2003), Plant Pathology: Phloeospora maculans leaf spot, Turkey - vein-limited brown spots with chlorotic halo
Florida DPI Plant Pathology Circular No. 329 (1990): Mycosphaerella mori - large dry necrotic circular spots
Texas A&M Plant Disease Handbook: leaf spots of mulberry (Cercospora spp.)
classes.research_note: 'Leaf spot' is a SYMPTOM-based grouping of many distinct pathogens. Visual classification cannot identify the causal species; this is documented as an inherent limitation.

classes.name: leaf_blight
classes.label: Leaf Blight
classes.description: Blight conditions of mulberry foliage represented by the bacterial blight symptom complex (primarily Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) and advanced coalescing fungal necrosis. The defining visual signature is the evolution from discrete water-soaked spots to EXPANDING/COALESCING irregular dead tissue: lesions enlarge, fuse into large necrotic areas (often scorched or tip/margin-originating), and are frequently ringed by chlorotic halos with water-soaked advancing margins.
visual_indicators: Early lesions are small WATER-SOAKED (olive/translucent) spots, often brown-black, frequently ANGULAR and ringed by a yellow (chlorotic) halo; shoots may show black striping
Lesions ENLARGE and COALESCE into large, irregular necrotic regions rather than remaining discrete (the coalescence + spread is the defining difference vs leaf spot)
Water-soaked lesion margins at the advancing edge (characteristic of bacterial blight) that later dry brown
Necrosis often starts at leaf tips/margins or along veins and scorches/withers most of the leaf
Affects young/tender leaves and shoot tips predominantly (cool, wet spring); shoot-tip wilting and dieback may accompany (may not be visible in a single-leaf photo)
classes.annotation_guidance: Use COALESCENCE as the primary discriminator: label leaf_blight when adjoining lesions FUSE into irregular joined necrotic zones (with/without water-soaked margins or yellow halos). A leaf with many lesions that REMAIN discrete and separated is leaf_spot, however numerous or severe. If a photo shows only part of the affected tissue, prefer needs_review over forcing a class. Bacterial vs fungal causation CANNOT be determined visually - the class is deliberately causal-agent-agnostic.
confounding_conditions: Coalesced leaf-spot lesions (documented in PMC10665727) appear blight-like - a major ambiguity; resolve by search for fused, haloed, water-soaked margins
Mild/early blight with only low-density discrete water-soaked spots matches the leaf_spot profile; if halos/angularity/distortion are present, weigh blight even at low lesion count
Drought/salt/wind scorch and herbicide injury mimic marginal necrosis
Late-stage rust causes whole-leaf withering that resembles blight
evidence_sources: Texas A&M Plant Disease Handbook: Bacterial Blight (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) - watersoaked spots, black shoot stripes, tip wilt
PNW Plant Disease Handbook: mulberry bacterial blight - small brown-black spots with yellow haloes, distorted leaves, bud damage, shoot necrosis/dieback, cankers with ooze

RHS 'Bacterial leaf spot' (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori): numerous small angular black leaf spots often with a yellow halo; whole leaves may turn yellow (NOTE: the SAME P. syringae pathology is published under both 'bacterial blight' and 'bacterial leaf spot' names - both belong to this bright symptom complex, and small angular spotted presentations overlap the leaf_spot class)
PlantVillage: mulberry bacterial blight - small black angular spots; large brown spots on leaves
Sahin (1999), first report: small water-soaked spots expanding to dark brown-black elongated lesions
Huang et al. (2025), Front. Plant Sci. 16:1517050: mulberry bacterial blight is a pathogen COMPLEX (P. syringae dominant among up to 10 confirmed bacteria); attacks young tender leaves/shoot tips
J-Stage (2014) 'Mulberry Diseases and Their Control': bacterial blight listed among serious mulberry diseases
Arunakumar et al. (2023): Bipolaris sorokiniana lesions coalesce into blightened appearance
Philippine Phytopathology (1995) Dizon & Kakishima: symptomatology of mulberry rust/blight complex caused by C. fici
classes.research_note: FLAGGED RESEARCH RISK: literature does not provide a single crisp visual definition separating blight from severe leaf spot on mulberry. EXPERT ADJUDICATION (Sep 2026): a domain expert reviewed all 100 test-lot LB_A leaves (labeled contact sheet at /tmp/LB_A_review) and CONFIRMED ALL are leaf blight - many are early/mild blight (single large or few discrete necrotic lesions; median necrotic coverage 0.032, p90 0.085), so halo/angular/water-soaked mild lesions must be weighed as blight even without gross coalescence. FAILURE MODE IS WITHIN-CLASS SEVERITY SHIFT, NOT MISLABEL: blight training lots C-E span mild-to-severe (median cov 0.10-0.12, p90 0.34-0.40) while test lot LB_A is uniform-low (p90 0.085) and collapses into leaf_spot (80/100). See Known Limitations in docs/dataset.md.
